newsitem.title: ITALY: Referendum fiasco stirs reform calls in Italy.
newsitem.headline: Referendum fiasco stirs reform calls in Italy.

text.p: Pressure built up in Italy on Monday for stricter rules on holding national referendums after an attempt to bring change through direct democracy proved a multi-million dollar flop.

Only 30 percent of Italy's 49 million voters took part in Sunday's seven referendums, way short of the 50 percent of the electorate required for such tests to be valid and the lowest turnout in any national ballot since 1945.

Mainstream politicians blamed the fiasco on the leader of the referendum movement, maverick civil rights campaigner Marco Pannella, accusing him of wasting the public's time and devaluing the balloting process for self-publicity.
Some even cautioned that the flop would further dent public faith in politics, already battered by the corruption scandals of the early 1990s and the subsequent slow pace of change.
Pannella and his supporters had championed six of the seven issues put before voters, covering topics as diverse as hunting, privatisation, journalism and the careers of magistrates.
The referendums, invalidated by the low turnout, cost Italy 840 billion lire ($490 million) to stage.

"You cannot call on the people to express themselves on issues that are marginal, confused, contradictory, perhaps very important but complicated, and tell them you're giving them back the sceptre of democracy," said Paolo Barile, a noted jurist.
"A referendum makes sense when it is a matter of deciding about a political or cultural turning point in the history of the republic," Barile told L'Unita newspaper.
Referendums have proved a valuable tool in Italian democracy, allowing voters to express a view on fundamental concerns that the country's unwieldly parliament has been unwilling or unable to tackle.

Italy's monarchy was abolished by referendum in 1946 and substantive policy on divorce, abortion, use of nuclear power and, to a certain degree, the electoral system has been formulated following plebiscites.
Recent years, however, have seen a flurry of referendums on highly technical issues, many of them promoted by Pannella and his Radical Party.

Eight took place on one day in 1993 and 12 on the same day in 1995, although Sunday's exercise was only the second time that a referendum had failed to obtain a quorum. The previous time was in 1990 on hunting and the use of pesticides.
By law, campaigners must obtain the signatures of 500,000 voters to put a petition to the Constitutional Court, which then rules whether the issue should go to a referendum.

Following Sunday's debacle, many politicians called for the threshold to be raised to 800,000 or one million signatures, a change that could come through a parliamentary commission examining constitutional reform.
"The intention is not to make it more difficult to hold a referendum," said Cesare Salvi, a member of the commission and lower house leader of the large Democratic Party of the Left.
"The aim is to make sure that attention is focused on a few issues because citizens have the right not to be buried under an avalanche of proposals."

Pannella, who shot to prominence in 1974 by leading opposition to a referendum that sought to ban divorce, was unrepentant despite the low turnout, vowing to press on with plans to seek more than 30 referendums next year.
